title: Identification evidence
subtitle: Code D procedures, the Turnbull guidelines, and vulnerable suspects
objectives: State when PACE Code D requires an identification procedure to be held, and identify the recognised forms it can take
Explain the Turnbull guidelines and the factors a court uses to assess the quality of disputed identification evidence
Explain the role of an appropriate adult where the suspect is a juvenile or otherwise vulnerable, and identify who qualifies

leadingAuthorities.citation: Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, Code D
leadingAuthorities.role: Governs when an identification procedure must be held, the forms it can take, and the safeguards for vulnerable suspects
Sets out the guidelines a trial judge must follow when disputed visual identification evidence is the whole or main basis of the case

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Identification evidence sounds like the strongest kind of proof — a witness pointing at the defendant and saying 'that's him'. It is also one of the most common causes of wrongful conviction. This lesson is where the practice catches up with that reality: procedure and scrutiny, not certainty.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the Code D categories and the Turnbull mnemonic. The test pool leans on fact patterns that hide a defective procedure or a weak identification inside an otherwise ordinary witness account — read for what's missing, not just what's there.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down on Parts 2 and 3. Before you can spot a flawed identification you need the four procedure types and the ADVOKATE factors cold — the rest of the lesson assumes you can list both without prompting.

overview.hook: A witness sees a man run from a burgled shop for four seconds, at dusk, from thirty metres away, through a wire fence. Three months later she picks him out of a video identification set with 'complete confidence'. Juries find that confidence compelling. The Court of Appeal has spent decades explaining why it shouldn't — because honesty and accuracy are not the same thing, and the law has built an entire procedural apparatus around the gap between them.

parts.heading: Why confident witnesses are still often wrong
parts.voice: argumentative — states the intuitive view, then dismantles it
body: The intuitive view of eyewitness evidence is that a witness either saw the defendant or didn't, and that a confident, honest witness is a reliable one. Decades of documented miscarriages of justice say otherwise: mistaken identification is the single largest contributing factor in proven wrongful convictions, and it is not correlated with how sure the witness sounds.

The reason is structural, not a matter of individual witnesses being careless or dishonest. Human memory for faces is reconstructive — it degrades with time, is distorted by stress, and is easily contaminated by suggestion (a photograph glimpsed afterwards, a description overheard, the mere fact of being shown one suspect rather than several). None of that shows up as hesitation in the witness box.

PACE 1984, Code D exists to manage this risk procedurally, by controlling how an identification is obtained so a court can later test its quality. R v Turnbull then supplies the substantive check: once a disputed identification is in evidence, the trial judge must direct the jury on exactly how much weight it can safely bear.

components.definition: A mandatory direction a judge gives a jury whenever the case against the defendant depends wholly or substantially on the correctness of one or more identifications the defence disputes, warning of the special need for caution and explaining why even an honest, convinced witness can be mistaken.

interaction.prompt: Does the reliability of an eyewitness's identification correlate strongly with how confident the witness appears when giving it?
options: No — confidence and accuracy are only weakly linked, which is exactly why the law treats ID evidence with special caution
Yes — a witness who is certain is, as a matter of psychology, reliably correct
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. That gap between confidence and accuracy is the entire reason Code D and Turnbull exist as separate, overlapping safeguards.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this is the core misconception the lesson is built to correct. A witness can be completely honest, completely confident, and still wrong, which is precisely why procedure and judicial direction matter more than demeanour.

parts.heading: When Code D requires a procedure, and the four forms it can take
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students will return to
body: Code D bites whenever a witness has identified, or may be able to identify, a suspect, and the suspect's identity is disputed — that is, the police have a named or located suspect but no unequivocal identification yet, and the suspect does not admit being the person seen. If identity is not in dispute (the suspect admits being at the scene and being seen), no procedure is required at all.

Where a procedure is required, Code D sets out four possible forms, and it prescribes an order of preference rather than leaving the choice open. Video identification is the default: the witness views a set of moving images, one of the suspect and at least eight others who resemble them. An identification parade (a physical line-up) may be offered instead where the suspect requests it and it is practicable. Group identification — observing the suspect in an informal group, such as at a shopping centre — is used where video identification or a parade isn't practicable. Confrontation, where the witness is shown the suspect alone and asked 'is this the person?', is the last resort, used only when none of the other three is practicable, because it carries the highest risk of suggestion.

The identifying officer running the procedure must have no involvement in the investigation, and the witness must not be shown photographs of the suspect or given any other indication of who to pick before the procedure takes place. A breach of these safeguards doesn't automatically exclude the resulting evidence, but it is a powerful basis for a defence application to exclude it under PACE s 78, and it will heavily colour any Turnbull direction that follows.

components.label: The four Code D procedures, in order of preference
points: Video identification — the default; suspect's moving image shown among at least eight similar others
Identification parade — physical line-up; used where the suspect requests it and it is practicable
Group identification — suspect observed within an informal group in a public setting
Confrontation — suspect shown to the witness alone; last resort only, when nothing else is practicable

interaction.prompt: Under Code D, which procedure is the prescribed default where a formal identification procedure is required and no reason exists to depart from it?
options: Confrontation
Identification parade
Video identification
Group identification
interaction.explanation: Video identification is the starting point under Code D; the other three are used, in descending order of preference, only where video identification is not practicable or the suspect validly requests a parade.

parts.heading: ADVOKATE: testing the quality of what the witness saw
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the Turnbull facts before naming the doctrine
body: R v Turnbull arose from a series of appeals where convictions had rested substantially on visual identification that the defence disputed. The Court of Appeal laid down guidelines every trial judge must follow in that situation: warn the jury of the special need for caution, explain why a mistaken witness can still be convincing, and direct the jury to examine closely the circumstances in which the identification was made.

Those circumstances are commonly organised into the mnemonic ADVOKATE: the Amount of time the witness had the suspect under observation; the Distance between them; the Visibility at the time (light, weather); any Obstruction to the view; whether the witness Knew the suspect or had seen them before; whether there was Any special reason to remember the individual; the Time lapse between observation and reporting to police; and any material Errors or discrepancies between the description first given and the suspect's actual appearance.

Where the identification evidence is poor — a fleeting, distant glimpse, with no supporting evidence — and the judge considers no reasonable jury could safely convict on it, Turnbull requires the judge to withdraw the case from the jury altogether. Where the quality is reasonable, the case can go to the jury, but only with the full warning. Supporting evidence (a confession, forensic evidence, opportunity plus motive) can make an otherwise weak identification safe to leave to the jury even though it cannot cure a genuinely poor one.

components.factsShort: A series of conjoined appeals where convictions rested substantially or wholly on disputed visual identification.
components.ratioShort: Where the case depends wholly or substantially on disputed identification evidence, the judge must warn the jury of the special need for caution and direct them to scrutinise the circumstances of the identification (ADVOKATE); where the quality is poor and unsupported, the case should be withdrawn from the jury.

expanded.facts: The Court of Appeal heard several appeals together, each turning on eyewitness identification that the defendant disputed, to lay down general guidance rather than decide each case on its own narrow facts.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Widgery CJ held that whenever the prosecution case depends wholly or substantially on the correctness of an identification which the defence alleges to be mistaken, the judge should warn the jury of the special need for caution, explain the reason for that need, and direct them to closely examine the circumstances in which the identification was made.
expanded.significance: Turnbull remains the controlling authority on jury directions for identification evidence and is tested constantly in SQE1 fact patterns that hide a poor-quality identification inside an otherwise unremarkable witness statement.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this witness account that most seriously weakens the quality of the identification under ADVOKATE.
interaction.scenarioText: A witness says she saw the man who snatched her bag for about eight seconds, in daylight, from four metres away, and recognised him immediately as a neighbour she has spoken to weekly for two years.
tappableSpans: recognised him immediately as a neighbour
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the weakest single factor here — but notice how the other facts (short distance, daylight, prior acquaintance) combine to make this a strong identification overall despite the brief observation.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at each ADVOKATE factor in isolation. Distance, visibility and prior knowledge are all favourable here; the observation time is comparatively short, which is the one factor working against reliability.

parts.heading: Vulnerable and young suspects: the appropriate adult
parts.voice: direct — sets out the safeguard plainly
body: A suspect who is a juvenile (under 18) or who is mentally vulnerable — because of a mental health condition, learning disability, or difficulty understanding the significance of what is happening — requires an appropriate adult (AA) to be present for key stages of the investigation, including an identification procedure. The purpose is not to advise on law (that is the solicitor's role) but to support, advise and assist the suspect, and to observe whether the process is being conducted properly and fairly.

The appropriate adult will typically be a parent or guardian, a social worker, or (failing either) another responsible adult who is not a police officer and not employed by the police. Crucially, someone cannot act as AA if they are also a suspect, victim, or witness in the same investigation, or if they have received admissions from the suspect in a professional capacity that could create a conflict.

For an identification procedure specifically, the AA's presence is a Code D requirement, not an optional courtesy: the police must inform the AA of what is proposed and allow them to be present, and their consent (or the parent/guardian's, for a juvenile) is required in addition to the suspect's own consent. A procedure run without the required AA safeguards is vulnerable to exclusion under s 78 in exactly the way a badly run video identification is.

components.definition: A parent, guardian, social worker or other responsible adult (never a police officer, and never someone with a conflicting role in the same case) whose presence is required at key investigative stages — including identification procedures — for a juvenile or mentally vulnerable suspect, to support and safeguard them, not to give legal advice.

interaction.prompt: A 16-year-old suspect's father is himself a witness who gave a statement about seeing the offence take place. Can the father act as the appropriate adult for his son's identification procedure?
options: Yes — a parent is always entitled to act as appropriate adult regardless of any other role
No — being a witness in the same investigation creates a conflict that disqualifies him from acting as AA
Yes, but only if the solicitor agrees
No — juveniles are never entitled to an appropriate adult for identification procedures
interaction.explanation: The AA safeguard exists to protect the suspect's interests without a competing role muddying that function. A parent who is also a witness in the same case has a conflicting position and cannot properly perform the AA role, so a substitute AA must be found.

parts.heading: Putting it together: procedure, quality, safeguard
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the combined problem before resolving it
body: In practice these three strands rarely arrive separately. A single fact pattern will usually test whether a procedure was required at all, whether the one used was correctly chosen and conducted, whether the resulting identification is strong or weak on ADVOKATE grounds, and — where the suspect is young or vulnerable — whether the appropriate adult safeguard was properly observed.

The trap is treating these as alternatives rather than as a stack: a technically compliant Code D procedure does not rescue a poor-quality identification from a Turnbull warning, and a strong identification does not excuse a missing appropriate adult. Each strand is assessed on its own terms, and a defence solicitor advising a client will typically be probing all three at once.
The two scenarios below both involve a disputed identification of a young suspect. Only one shows the procedural safeguards actually working as Code D intends.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that because a witness sounds confident and consistent, any procedural shortcuts in how the identification was obtained are unlikely to matter.
components.whyItsWrong: Confidence is not evidence of accuracy, and Code D compliance is assessed independently of how convincing the witness later appears. A confident but procedurally tainted identification is still vulnerable to exclusion, and the Turnbull direction still applies in full.

interaction.prompt: Two scenarios involving a 15-year-old suspect. In which was the identification procedure properly conducted?
interaction.scenarioA: The police arrange a video identification, notify the suspect's mother as appropriate adult in advance, and she is present and consents before the procedure begins.
interaction.scenarioB: The police show the witness a custody photograph of the suspect the day before, then proceed with a video identification with the suspect's mother present.
interaction.explanation: In A, both the AA safeguard and the correct procedural form are observed. In B, showing the witness a prior photograph of the suspect fatally contaminates the identification regardless of the AA's presence — a classic Code D breach that will support exclusion under s 78.

testPool.prompt: A named suspect is located by police, but no witness has yet identified them and the suspect denies being at the scene. Does Code D require an identification procedure?
options: Yes — identity is disputed and a witness may be able to identify the suspect, so a procedure is required
No — Code D only applies once the suspect has already confessed
No — Code D only applies to offences carrying a custodial sentence
Yes, but only if the suspect requests one
testPool.explanation: Code D is triggered where a witness has identified, or may be able to identify, a suspect and the suspect's identity is disputed. Denial of presence at the scene is a paradigm case of disputed identity.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is the prescribed order of preference for identification procedures under Code D, from most to least preferred?
options: Confrontation, group identification, identification parade, video identification
Video identification, identification parade, group identification, confrontation
Identification parade, video identification, confrontation, group identification
All four procedures are equally available and the choice is entirely at the officer's discretion
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes assume a parade is the 'gold standard' and therefore the default. Code D actually starts from video identification as the default, moving down the list only where that is not practicable or a valid parade request is made — confrontation is always the last resort.

testPool.prompt: A suspect requests an identification parade instead of a video identification. The custody officer refuses without giving any reason and proceeds straight to video identification. What is the significance of this?
options: None — the choice of procedure is always entirely at the officer's discretion
The suspect's request should be accommodated where practicable, and an unreasoned refusal may support a defence application to exclude the resulting evidence
It is irrelevant because only confrontation requires a stated reason
The identification is automatically inadmissible regardless of its quality
testPool.explanation: Code D allows a suspect to request a parade in place of video identification, and it should be arranged where practicable. Ignoring that request without justification undermines compliance with Code D and can ground a s 78 exclusion argument, though it does not make the evidence automatically inadmissible.

testPool.prompt: A witness is shown the suspect alone, in person, and asked 'is this the man who robbed you?' Which Code D procedure is this, and what is its status?
options: Group identification — the standard procedure for street robberies
Confrontation — a last-resort procedure used only where the other three are not practicable
Video identification — acceptable in any circumstances
Identification parade — used whenever the suspect declines to cooperate
testPool.explanation: Showing a witness the suspect alone and directly is confrontation. Because it carries the highest risk of suggestion, Code D restricts it to cases where video identification, a parade and group identification are all impracticable.

testPool.prompt: A witness observed the offender for fifteen seconds at close range in good light and had met him twice before. On disputed identification evidence like this, what direction must the trial judge give the jury?
options: No direction is needed because the identification is clearly strong
The full Turnbull direction, warning of the special need for caution, even though the quality here is good
A direction only if the defence specifically requests one
A direction that the jury must accept the identification as conclusive
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes think a strong-looking identification removes the need for a Turnbull warning. It does not — the warning is required whenever the case depends wholly or substantially on disputed identification evidence, regardless of how good that evidence appears; the quality only affects whether the case can safely go to the jury at all, not whether the warning is given.

testPool.prompt: The only evidence against the defendant is a fleeting glimpse, at night, from fifty metres, by a witness who had never seen the defendant before. There is no other supporting evidence. What should happen to the case?
options: The judge should give the standard Turnbull warning and let the jury decide as usual
The judge should withdraw the case from the jury because the identification evidence is poor and unsupported
The case should proceed because eyewitness evidence is always sufficient on its own
The judge should direct the jury to convict
testPool.explanation: Turnbull requires withdrawal from the jury where the quality of a disputed identification is poor and there is no supporting evidence to make it safe. A distant, brief, night-time glimpse of a stranger, standing alone, is the paradigm case for withdrawal.

testPool.prompt: What does the ADVOKATE mnemonic help a court assess?
options: Whether a confession was obtained oppressively
The quality of the circumstances in which a disputed identification was made
Whether bail should be granted
Whether a suspect is fit to be interviewed
testPool.explanation: ADVOKATE (Amount of time, Distance, Visibility, Obstruction, Known before, Any reason to remember, Time lapse, Errors) structures the Turnbull assessment of how reliable a disputed identification is likely to be.

testPool.prompt: A witness gave police an initial description of the offender as clean-shaven and of average height. The suspect eventually identified has a full beard and is noticeably tall. What is the significance of this discrepancy under Turnbull?
options: It is irrelevant because descriptions are never precise
It is a material 'Errors' factor under ADVOKATE that weakens the identification and should be highlighted to the jury
It automatically renders the identification inadmissible
It only matters if the suspect raises an alibi defence
testPool.explanation: A significant mismatch between the description first given and the suspect's actual appearance is the 'Errors' limb of ADVOKATE and is a key factor a Turnbull direction requires the jury to weigh when assessing reliability.

testPool.prompt: Under Code D, who is disqualified from acting as the identifying officer who conducts a video identification procedure?
options: Any officer holding the rank of sergeant or above
An officer involved in the investigation of the offence
Any officer who has previously interviewed the suspect on an unrelated matter
There is no restriction on which officer may conduct the procedure
testPool.explanation: Code D requires the identifying officer to have no involvement in the investigation, to keep the procedure independent of the officers building the case and reduce the risk of conscious or unconscious steering of the witness.

testPool.prompt: A 17-year-old suspect's identification procedure is arranged, and his older brother — who has no involvement in the case — is asked to attend as appropriate adult. Is this acceptable?
options: No — only a parent or social worker can ever act as appropriate adult
Yes — a responsible adult with no conflicting role in the case can act as AA where a parent or guardian is unavailable
No — a suspect's own family member can never act as AA
Yes, but only with the investigating officer's approval
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes assume the AA role is limited to parents or professionals. In fact any responsible adult who is not a police officer and has no conflicting role in the investigation can act as AA, which commonly includes another family member where a parent is unavailable.

testPool.prompt: A suspect has a diagnosed learning disability affecting her understanding of formal procedures, but she is 34 years old. Does Code D require an appropriate adult for her identification procedure?
options: No — the appropriate adult safeguard only applies to suspects under 18
Yes — mentally vulnerable adults require an appropriate adult regardless of age
No — only suspects who are unrepresented require an appropriate adult
Yes, but only if she is also unrepresented
testPool.explanation: The appropriate adult requirement covers both juveniles and mentally vulnerable suspects of any age, where vulnerability affects their ability to understand the significance of what is happening or to safeguard their own interests.

testPool.prompt: What is the correct characterisation of the appropriate adult's function during an identification procedure?
options: To provide legal advice on whether the suspect should consent to the procedure
To support, advise and assist the suspect, and to observe that the procedure is conducted properly and fairly
To formally represent the suspect in place of a solicitor
To decide, on the suspect's behalf, which procedure should be used
testPool.explanation: The appropriate adult's role is welfare and fairness oversight, not legal advice — that remains the solicitor's function. The AA supports the suspect and watches for procedural unfairness.

testPool.prompt: A defence solicitor discovers that a witness was briefly shown a custody photograph of the suspect before an otherwise correctly run video identification. What is the most likely consequence?
options: None — the video identification itself was compliant, so the prior photograph is irrelevant
The identification is strengthened, because the witness had already formed a view
The defence has a strong basis to apply to exclude the identification evidence under s 78, because the prior photograph risks contaminating the result
The witness must be treated as an unreliable witness for all purposes in the trial
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to focus only on whether the formal procedure itself was run correctly. But Code D compliance is assessed on the whole process, and showing the witness the suspect's image beforehand contaminates an otherwise compliant procedure — this is one of the most commonly tested breaches.

testPool.prompt: In a video identification, how many other individuals must resemble the suspect and appear alongside them in the set of images shown to the witness, at minimum?
options: At least eight
At least three
At least fifteen
There is no minimum number
testPool.explanation: Code D requires the suspect's image to be shown alongside images of at least eight other people who resemble them in age, general appearance and position in life, so the witness is not steered towards any one individual.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating procedure, evidential quality and the appropriate adult safeguard as substitutes for one another. A compliant procedure does not cure a weak identification; a strong identification does not excuse a missing appropriate adult. Check all three, every time.
